teaser: She has just let go of the chain. Two of her three candles are already out.
review_notes:
The claim that this is among Tate's best-selling postcards is widely repeated; worth confirming before publishing.
Candles: the standard reading is two blown out and one still burning; in this reproduction the flame on the left candle is faint.
Influence of French open-air painting (Bastien-Lepage) on the brushwork is the usual art-historical reading.
Waterhouse's three Shalott paintings: 1888 (Tate), 1894 (Leeds), 1915 (Art Gallery of Ontario).

lesson.text: This canvas is two meters wide, about six and a half feet. Stand in front of it at Tate Britain and the woman in the boat is close to your own size, sitting at your own height. Waterhouse wanted you on the riverbank with her, near enough to hear the reeds scrape the hull.

Her story comes from a poem by Alfred Tennyson that most Victorian readers knew by heart. A lady lives alone in a tower on the island of Shalott, upstream from Camelot. A curse forbids her to look at the world directly. She may only watch it in a mirror, and weave what she sees there into a tapestry.

One day the knight Lancelot rides through the mirror, singing. She turns and looks out of the window. The mirror cracks. Knowing the curse has fallen on her, she goes down to the river, finds a boat and lets the current carry her toward Camelot. She will die before she gets there.
Waterhouse chose the exact second of departure. Something still ties the boat to the bank. Can you find what she is letting go of?

spots.title: The chain
spots.text: Her right hand holds the mooring chain, loose, about to drop. In the poem this is one line: “She loosed the chain, and down she lay.” The painting stretches that single gesture into a whole scene.

lesson.text: So nothing has happened yet, and everything is decided. That is why the picture feels so still. Painters before Waterhouse had usually shown the dramatic moment in the tower, with the cracking mirror and flying threads. He picked the quiet one, and it is the quiet one people remember.
Tennyson's lady sings as she drifts, “a carol, mournful, holy,” and the people on the banks hear her voice fade. Waterhouse paints her lips parted. She is in the middle of her last song.

The far end of the boat is where he tells you how it ends. Poems can say “she died.” A painting has to find objects that say it. Follow the dark hull to the right, toward the prow, the pointed front of the boat.

lesson.title: The prow
lesson.text: Three objects sit at the front of the boat. Together they turn it into something close to a floating coffin.

spots.title: Three candles
spots.text: Three candles stand in the wind. Two have already gone out, and the last flame leans sideways. Victorian viewers read candles as a life burning down: hers is two-thirds spent.

spots.title: The crucifix
spots.text: A small pale figure of Christ on the cross lies in front of the candles, facing her. With it, the boat becomes a kind of altar, and her journey a funeral she is attending alive.

spots.title: The lantern
spots.text: A lantern hangs under the carved, gilded prow. The light is fading: in the poem she sets out as the day closes, and she will be floating in the dark before long.

lesson.text: None of these three objects is in Tennyson. The poem mentions only the boat and the name she writes on it. Waterhouse invented the candles, the crucifix and the lantern because a picture needs props where a poem can use a sentence.

He also brought along the one thing she made. In the poem the tapestry stays behind in the tower. Here she has dragged it into the boat and sits on it, its edge trailing in the water. Years of work, woven from reflections, about to be ruined.

lesson.title: What she wove
lesson.text: The tapestry hangs over the side like a picture inside the picture. Its roundels show what her mirror showed her.

spots.title: Knights on horseback
spots.text: In the large roundel, riders pass in a group. These are the people she watched go by toward Camelot for years, without ever being able to look at them directly.

spots.title: The tower
spots.text: Lower down, a smaller scene shows a woman in front of gray castle walls: herself, perhaps, at the tower she has just left. The wet hem of the cloth is already in the river.

lesson.text: Waterhouse could not leave this story alone. He painted the Lady three times over 27 years, and oddly in reverse order: first her death voyage, then the moment she looks at Lancelot, and last, in 1915, the years of weaving that came before.

Now the surroundings. The reeds in the left corner are slashed in with thick, quick strokes, and the far bank dissolves into soft gray-green. This is not the hard, every-leaf precision of the first Pre-Raphaelites, the young English painters who in 1848 swore to paint nature in sharp detail.

Waterhouse was born in 1849, a year after that group formed, so he belongs to the next generation. He kept their love of medieval legends and red-haired heroines, and mixed it with the looser handling French painters were using to work outdoors. Critics in 1888 noticed the French accent at once.
Old stories, new brush: Waterhouse took a Pre-Raphaelite subject and painted it with the broad, outdoor touch of his own time. That mix is his signature.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Chin lifted, eyes lowered and unfocused, lips apart. She is singing, and she is not looking at anything anymore.

spots.title: The reeds
spots.text: Each reed is a single loaded stroke of ochre or brown. From across the room they look sharp. Up close they are almost abstract.

spots.title: A swallow
spots.text: A dark bird skims the water at the left edge, and another flies lower down among the reeds. They are the only things moving freely in the picture.

spots.title: A fallen leaf
spots.text: One dry leaf has landed on her white lap. The trees are turning rust and gold: it is autumn, the season when things end.

spots.title: The only sky
spots.text: A single patch of daylight and open hillside, far off in the corner she has her back to. Everything around her is shade.

spots.title: White dress
spots.text: Her dress is the brightest thing on the canvas, set against the darkest trees. Waterhouse makes her glow like the last candle.

lesson.text: The sugar merchant Henry Tate bought the painting and included it in the gift of pictures that founded the gallery now called Tate Britain. It has hung in that collection since 1894.

It has rarely been out of favor with visitors since, even in the decades when critics dismissed Victorian painting as sentimental. Perhaps because the question it asks has not aged. She was safe as long as she only watched life in a mirror. She looked anyway. Would you?

quiz.question: What exact moment of the story does Waterhouse show?
options: The mirror cracking in the tower
The lady releasing the boat's chain
quiz.explanation: Her right hand holds the mooring chain, about to let it drop.

quiz.question: What do the candles at the prow suggest?
options: Her life is almost burned out
quiz.explanation: Two of the three are already out, a sign that her life is nearly spent.

quiz.question: Which objects did Waterhouse add that are not in Tennyson's poem?
quiz.explanation: The poem mentions only the boat and her name on it; the painter invented the props.

quiz.question: How does this painting differ from the first Pre-Raphaelites' work?
options: Its brushwork is looser, with a French outdoor touch
quiz.explanation: Waterhouse kept their subjects but painted the reeds and bank with broad, quick strokes.

quiz.question: What is shown on the cloth hanging over the boat?
options: Scenes she saw in her mirror
quiz.explanation: It is her tapestry, woven from the reflections of people passing toward Camelot.

facts.text: Waterhouse painted the Lady of Shalott three times.
facts.explanation: He returned to the story in 1888, 1894 and 1915.

facts.text: The painting is small enough to hold in two hands.
facts.explanation: It is about two meters wide, and the figure is close to life size.

facts.text: In the painting, the lady is shown in the middle of a song.
facts.explanation: Her lips are parted: in the poem she sings as she drifts away.
